title: Reciprocal rank fusion — Composite Search Engine
description: RRF scores each document by summing 1/(k + rank) over the rankings that include it. It needs no score normalization because ranks, not raw scores, are fused. RRF is the default unsupervised fusion: simple, robust, and hard to beat.

title: Score normalization — Composite Search Engine
description: Fusing raw scores requires normalization: min-max scaling or z-scores per ranker. Without it, the ranker with the widest score range dominates. Normalization is the unglamorous step that makes fusion work.
provenance: Public methodology — standard computer-science technique documented in the technical literature; fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: Weighted linear combination — Composite Search Engine
description: Weighted sums let operators favor trusted rankers: 0.7*keyword + 0.3*phonetic. Weights are tuned on labeled data via grid or coordinate search. Weights encode which signals the application trusts.
provenance: Public methodology — standard computer-science technique documented in the technical literature; fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: Cascade ranking — Composite Search Engine
description: Cascades run a cheap ranker first, then an expensive one only on the top candidates. Keyword retrieval feeds neural reranking on the top 100. Cascades buy quality at bounded cost.
provenance: Public methodology — standard computer-science technique documented in the technical literature; fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: Borda count fusion — Composite Search Engine
description: Borda assigns points by position (n-1 for first) and sums across rankings. It is a voting-theoretic fusion needing no scores at all. Borda is simple but sensitive to weak rankers' noise.
provenance: Public methodology — standard computer-science technique documented in the technical literature; fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: CombSUM and CombMNZ — Composite Search Engine
description: CombSUM adds normalized scores; CombMNZ multiplies the sum by the number of rankers retrieving the document. MNZ rewards documents found by many methods, a consensus bonus. These classic fusions remain strong baselines.

title: Learning to rank — Composite Search Engine
description: Supervised fusion trains a model on (query, document, label) triples with per-ranker scores as features. Gradient-boosted trees over ranker scores dominate benchmarks. Learning to rank turns fusion into a prediction problem.

title: Query-type routing — Composite Search Engine
description: Not every query needs every ranker: routers send name queries to phonetic+typo rankers and topic queries to semantic ones. Routing saves compute and reduces noise from irrelevant rankers. Smart routing beats always-on fusion on both speed and quality.

title: Diversified fusion — Composite Search Engine
description: Fusion can over-concentrate on one interpretation; diversification re-ranks for aspect coverage. MMR-style penalties demote near-duplicates of already-selected results. Diversity matters most for ambiguous queries.

title: Federated search merging — Composite Search Engine
description: Federated search queries independent collections, each with its own ranker and score scale. Merging needs score calibration or rank-based fusion like RRF. Federation keeps sources autonomous while presenting one list.

title: Fallback chains — Composite Search Engine
description: When the primary ranker returns too few results, fallbacks relax the query: fewer terms, typo tolerance, broader fields. Each fallback stage widens the net until the result count suffices. Fallbacks guarantee users rarely face an empty page.

title: Evaluating fused systems — Composite Search Engine
description: Fusion is judged against each component alone: it must beat the best single ranker to justify its complexity. Ablation removes one ranker at a time to measure marginal value. Honest evaluation keeps fusion lean.

title: Real-time fusion budgets — Composite Search Engine
